2026 · Research Note 9

Can machine vision teach us what the voltage noise of gas-evolving electrodes means?

A lightweight CNN tracks microbubbles optically, creating a baseline that lets frequency-domain voltage analysis recover characteristic bubble residence times.

In brief

QuestionCan machine vision teach us what the voltage noise of gas-evolving electrodes means?
ResultBubble residence times obtained from optical tracking agreed with features in the electrochemical voltage signal, and the frequency method was extended to gauzes, foams, and felts at industrial current densities.
Why it mattersAI provides the ground truth needed to convert a difficult visual phenomenon into a simpler electrochemical diagnostic.
Using Machine Learning and In Situ Microscopy to Track Microbubble Dynamics during Electrolysis
Jonathan Quintal et al. · ACS Electrochemistry · Published 8 April 2026
DOI: 10.1021/acselectrochem.6c00030

The electrochemical problem

Gas bubbles can block active area, alter local resistance, and change mass transport during electrolysis. Yet directly measuring bubble dynamics on porous transport layers under realistic operation is difficult because many bubbles appear, merge, detach, and obscure one another.

The paper uses a simpler optical system first to ask a useful diagnostic question: can bubble motion detected by microscopy be linked to a signature already present in the electrical signal?

What the researchers did

A lightweight convolutional neural network was used to track microbubbles on a platinum ultramicroelectrode. The resulting optical trajectories provided characteristic residence times that could be treated as a reference measurement.

The authors then analyzed the voltage signal in the frequency domain and compared its characteristic times with the optically measured bubble dynamics. After establishing that connection, they translated the frequency-domain approach to commercial-type electrode geometries including gauzes, foams, and felts.

What they found

The characteristic bubble residence times extracted from optical tracking were reflected in the voltage fluctuations. On complex porous electrodes with multiple simultaneous bubbles, the authors used a weighted average of the frequency spectrum to obtain a lumped characteristic time for the overall bubble dynamics.

This made it possible to extend the diagnostic to electrodes operating at industrially relevant current densities where direct tracking of every individual bubble is no longer practical.

Why this matters

The clever role of machine learning here is not to become the final sensor. Computer vision provides a quantitative optical baseline that reveals how bubble dynamics appear in an ordinary electrochemical observable.

Once that mapping is established, a simpler electrical diagnostic may be used in geometries where microscopy is difficult. This is a useful pattern for AI in electrochemistry: use a rich measurement to teach the meaning of a cheaper one.

One important caution

The frequency-domain signal on a porous electrode represents many bubbles at once. The lumped characteristic time therefore does not retain all of the individual bubble information available from microscopy.

The method should be interpreted as a system-level descriptor of bubble dynamics, not as a complete reconstruction of every nucleation, coalescence, and detachment event.

Primary source

Jonathan Quintal et al. Using Machine Learning and In Situ Microscopy to Track Microbubble Dynamics during Electrolysis. ACS Electrochemistry (2026). DOI: 10.1021/acselectrochem.6c00030.
